section.title: The Guilt Offering
section.sectionRationale: Closing the sacrificial law collection's fifth offering, this passage first lists specific cases requiring a sin offering, scaled for the poor and poorest, then introduces the guilt offering, which uniquely requires restitution, repaying what was wrongly taken plus a fifth, alongside the sacrifice.
section.thesis: God provides atonement scaled to what a sinner can afford, from a lamb down to a handful of flour, for specific unintentional sins, and where sin has actually damaged another person or defrauded God's holy things, He requires not only sacrifice but full restitution plus a fifth, showing that true repentance repairs as well as atones.
section.frameNote: Four movements: specific cases requiring a sin offering; the sliding scale of provision for the poor; the guilt offering for sins against holy things; and the guilt offering for sins of deception and fraud against a neighbor, requiring restitution.

verses.text: “If someone sins by failing to testify when he hears a public charge about something he has witnessed, whether he has seen it or learned of it, he shall bear the iniquity.
Or if a person touches anything {{tame|unclean}}, whether the carcass of any unclean wild animal or livestock or crawling creature, even if he is unaware of it, he is unclean and guilty.
Or if he touches human uncleanness, anything by which one becomes unclean, even if he is unaware of it, when he realizes it, he is guilty.

Or if someone swears thoughtlessly with his lips to do anything good or evil, in whatever matter a man may rashly pronounce an oath, even if he is unaware of it, when he realizes it, he is guilty in the matter.
If someone incurs guilt in one of these ways, he must confess the sin he has committed,

units.label: Scaled to what the sinner can afford
units.note: a lamb, two birds, or fine flour

verses.text: and he must bring his {{asham|guilt offering}} to the LORD for the sin he has committed: a female lamb or goat from the flock as a sin offering. And the priest will make atonement for him concerning his sin.
If, however, he cannot afford a lamb, he may bring to the LORD as restitution for his sin two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering.
He is to bring them to the priest, who shall first present the one for the sin offering. He is to twist its head at the front of its neck without severing it;
then he is to sprinkle some of the blood of the sin offering on the side of the altar, while the rest of the blood is drained out at the base of the altar. It is a sin offering.
And the priest must prepare the second bird as a burnt offering according to the ordinance. In this way the priest will make atonement for him for the sin he has committed, and he will be forgiven.

But if he cannot afford two turtledoves or two young pigeons, he may bring a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a sin offering. He must not put olive oil or frankincense on it, because it is a sin offering.
He is to bring it to the priest, who shall take a handful from it as a memorial portion and burn it on the altar atop the offerings made by fire to the LORD; it is a sin offering.
In this way the priest will make atonement for him for any of these sins he has committed, and he will be forgiven. The remainder will belong to the priest, like the grain offering.”

units.label: Guilt against the LORD's holy things

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,

“If someone acts unfaithfully and sins unintentionally against any of the LORD's holy things, he must bring his guilt offering to the LORD: an unblemished ram from the flock, of proper value in silver shekels according to the sanctuary shekel; it is a guilt offering.

Regarding any holy thing he has harmed, he must make restitution by adding a fifth of its value to it and giving it to the priest, who will make atonement on his behalf with the ram as a guilt offering, and he will be forgiven.
If someone sins and violates any of the LORD's commandments even though he was unaware, he is guilty and shall bear his punishment.

He is to bring to the priest an unblemished ram of proper value from the flock as a guilt offering. Then the priest will make atonement on his behalf for the wrong he has committed in ignorance, and he will be forgiven.
It is a guilt offering; he was certainly guilty before the LORD.”
And the LORD said to Moses,
“If someone sins and acts unfaithfully against the LORD by deceiving his neighbor in regard to a deposit or security entrusted to him or stolen, or if he extorts his neighbor
or finds lost property and lies about it and swears falsely, or if he commits any such sin that a man might commit,
once he has sinned and becomes guilty, he must return what he has stolen or taken by extortion, or the deposit entrusted to him, or the lost property he found,
or anything else about which he has sworn falsely. He must make restitution in full, add a fifth of the value, and pay it to the owner on the day he acknowledges his guilt.
Then he must bring to the priest his guilt offering to the LORD: an unblemished ram of proper value from the flock.
In this way the priest will make atonement for him before the LORD, and he will be forgiven for anything he may have done to incur guilt.”

tame.gloss: Unclean, ceremonially defiled. Contact with certain carcasses or human uncleanness rendered a person tame even without any conscious awareness, showing that defilement, like sin, can be real regardless of whether a person notices it happening.

asham.gloss: The guilt offering, distinct from the sin offering, chattat, in that it specifically addresses sins that have caused measurable harm or defrauded holy things or a neighbor, requiring restitution in addition to sacrifice.

basic.context: This passage closes the sacrificial law's first collection. It first lists specific cases, failing to testify, touching something unclean, or a rash oath, that require a sin offering, scaled generously down to a handful of flour for the very poor. Then it introduces the guilt offering, required whenever sin has caused actual damage, either to God's holy things or to a neighbor's property, and this offering always comes with restitution, repaying what was taken plus a fifth.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes Israel's actual old covenant provisions for atonement and restitution; it is not a legal code for Christians to reenact today. Its abiding truth is that God's mercy scales down to whatever the poorest sinner can bring, and that genuine repentance includes repairing the actual harm done, not sacrifice alone.
basic.originalLanguages: Even unnoticed contact with something tame, unclean, created real guilt, showing that defilement does not depend on awareness. The asham, guilt offering, is distinguished from the ordinary chattat, sin offering, because it specifically addresses damage done, whether against God's holy things or a neighbor's property, and always requires restitution alongside the sacrifice.
basic.typology: The sliding scale, lamb, then birds, then flour, pictures a God who meets sinners exactly where their means allow, anticipating a gospel with no economic barrier to entry. The requirement of restitution plus a fifth foreshadows the New Testament pattern of repentance that includes making things right, as seen in Zacchaeus's fourfold repayment, Luke 19:8.
basic.christ: Christ is the guilt offering, asham, that Isaiah 53:10 foretells, the Servant whose life is made an offering for guilt, so that our account with God is not only forgiven but genuinely settled, restitution paid in full by Him on our behalf.
basic.god: God's justice requires that actual harm be repaired, not merely apologized for, yet His mercy provides an offering within reach of every sinner regardless of wealth. He is neither an indifferent judge who overlooks real damage nor a God whose provision for atonement excludes the poor.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 53:10 calls the Suffering Servant's life a guilt offering, asham, made for our sin. Luke 19:8 shows Zacchaeus's repentance including fourfold restitution, echoing this pattern of repair alongside confession. 1 John 1:9 promises forgiveness and cleansing to those who confess.
basic.oneStory: This passage shows a God who provides atonement scaled to what every sinner can afford and who requires that real harm be genuinely repaired, not merely forgiven in word. It anticipates Christ, our guilt offering, whose sacrifice both forgives our sin and settles our account with God completely.

context.literary:
The passage has two halves, and the seam between them is marked by the speech formula of Leviticus 5:14, 'Then the LORD said to Moses,' repeated at 6:1. Leviticus 5:1-13 still belongs to the sin offering of chapter 4; it applies that offering to particular lapses and then provides for those who cannot afford it. Leviticus 5:14 to 6:7 introduces a new sacrifice, the asham, and gives it three cases of its own.

The first half opens with four short cases, verses 1 to 4, each introduced by 'if' or 'or if.' A man keeps silent when he is called to testify; a person touches an unclean carcass; someone touches human uncleanness; someone swears rashly. What links them is not the act itself but its lapse from memory. The refrain 'even if he is unaware of it, when he realizes it, he is guilty' runs through verses 2 to 4. The problem is a failure left unattended until it surfaces.

Then comes a descending ladder of provision in verses 6 to 13: a female lamb or goat, then two birds, then a tenth of an ephah of flour. Each step opens with 'if he cannot afford,' verses 7 and 11, and each step ends with the same outcome, atonement and forgiveness, verses 10 and 13. The rite gets smaller; the result does not.

The second half runs a parallel progression. Verses 14 to 16 concern wrongs against 'the LORD's holy things,' verses 17 to 19 a violation the offender cannot even identify, and 6:1-7 wrongs against a neighbour. The surprise is at 6:2, where defrauding a neighbour is described as acting 'unfaithfully against the LORD.' The two tables of the law meet in one sentence. The section ends in 6:7 with a sweeping promise, forgiveness 'for anything he may have done to incur guilt,' which closes the book's opening manual of offerings for the worshiper before chapters 6 and 7 turn to instructions for the priests.
context.historical:
Israel had no banks, insurance or police. Wealth was kept in animals, grain, silver and goods, and when a man travelled or needed safekeeping he left his property with a neighbour. Exodus 22:7-11 shows how disputes over such deposits were handled: by judges, and when no witness existed, by 'an oath before the LORD.' A false oath in such a case, Leviticus 6:3 and 6:5, was therefore a double crime. It robbed the neighbour and used the name of God to cover the theft.

Lost property was covered by the same trust. Deuteronomy 22:1-3 commands an Israelite who finds a neighbour's animal or cloak to keep it safe and return it. Leviticus 6:3 imagines the man who finds it and 'lies about it.'

The 'public charge' of 5:1 reflects a practice in which a wronged person or a court pronounced a solemn curse on anyone who knew the truth and did not come forward. Judges 17:2 shows a mother uttering such a curse over stolen silver, and Proverbs 29:24 describes the accomplice who 'receives the oath, but does not testify.' Silence under such a charge was itself sin.

The 'holy things' of 5:15 were whatever belonged to the sanctuary: tithes, firstfruits, the priests' portions, dedicated gifts. An Israelite might eat holy food by mistake, Leviticus 22:14, or keep back what was owed. The ram was assessed 'in silver shekels according to the sanctuary shekel,' a standard weight kept at the sanctuary, and the BSB footnote puts a shekel at about 11.4 grams of silver.

The poorest offering, a tenth of an ephah of flour, is the same measure as an omer, Exodus 16:36, the daily ration of manna for one person, Exodus 16:16. The destitute offered one day's bread.
context.canonical:
Numbers 5:5-8 restates the law of Leviticus 6:1-7 and adds two details: the offender 'must confess the sin he has committed,' and if the wronged person has died with no relative to receive the payment, 'the restitution belongs to the LORD.' Leviticus 22:14 applies the added fifth to a priest's family eating holy food in error.

The asham appears in striking places. The Philistines return the ark with 'a guilt offering' of gold, 1 Samuel 6:3, a pagan people recognising that a wrong against God's holy things needed compensation. In Ezra's day the men who had married foreign wives confessed their unfaithfulness and 'presented a ram from the flock as a guilt offering,' Ezra 10:19, using the word ma'al of Leviticus 5:15 for their sin, Ezra 10:10.

The most important use is Isaiah 53:10: 'when His soul is made a guilt offering, He will see His offspring.' The Servant does not simply die for sin; He becomes the reparation offering that repays what sin had stolen from God. The surrounding verses use the language of bearing iniquity, 'He bore the sin of many,' Isaiah 53:12, that Leviticus 5:1 and 5:17 attach to the guilty.

The poor person's provision appears in the Gospels. When Mary brought her firstborn to the temple, the family offered 'a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons,' Luke 2:24, the concession of Leviticus 12:8 for those who 'cannot afford a lamb,' matching the concession of Leviticus 5:7. Jesus' teaching on reconciliation before offering a gift, Matthew 5:23-24, keeps the order of Leviticus 6:5-6: first make it right with your neighbour, then come to the altar. Zacchaeus's promise to repay fourfold, Luke 19:8, reaches past this chapter's fifth to the fourfold penalty for a stolen sheep in Exodus 22:1.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to see that sin often hides in neglect. The man who stays silent, the person who forgets he touched something unclean, the one who blurts out an oath and moves on: none of them planned rebellion, but each left something unattended that God had not forgotten. The chapter teaches Israel to deal with such things when they come to mind, and to name them in confession, 5:5.

He also wanted Israel to know that no one was priced out of forgiveness. Poverty could not be an excuse for staying unforgiven, and it could not be a barrier to being forgiven. The rules were written so that the poorest Israelite, with a day's flour, went home with the same promise as a man who brought a lamb.

Finally, Moses wanted Israel to grasp that wronging a neighbour is wronging God. The laws on fraud sit under the heading of unfaithfulness against the LORD, 6:2, and the order is fixed: restore what was taken, add a fifth, pay it that same day, and only then bring the ram. Israel was to learn that the altar is no substitute for honesty, and that worship without restitution is not accepted.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The sacrificial provisions were commands for Israel under the Sinai covenant, and Christians do not bring rams or flour for sin, because Christ's sacrifice has fulfilled them, Hebrews 10:10-14. The civil detail, such as the exact rate of a fifth, belonged to Israel's legal order.

Two principles carry straight over. Confession is still commanded: 'If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us,' 1 John 1:9, and believers are to confess to one another, James 5:16. And restitution is still the fruit of real repentance. Jesus tells worshipers to be reconciled before offering their gift, Matthew 5:23-24, and Zacchaeus shows what repentance looks like when it reaches the wallet, Luke 19:8. A Christian who has cheated someone is not free simply to pray about it; where the wrong can be repaired, love requires that it be repaired, generously.

debates.question: Why does restitution require repaying the value plus an additional fifth, rather than the exact amount taken?

views.label: A penalty that discourages theft and deception
views.case: The added fifth functions as a penalty beyond simple repayment, making dishonesty costly rather than merely neutral once discovered.

views.label: Compensation for loss of use and trust
views.case: Others see the added fifth as compensating the wronged party for the time their property was withheld and the trust that was broken, beyond the item's bare value.

views.label: A reduced penalty that rewards confession
views.case: A third view compares this law with Exodus 22:4 and 22:7-9, where a thief caught with the goods pays double. Leviticus 6:4-5 concerns a man who 'acknowledges his guilt' himself. On this reading the fifth is lighter than the court's penalty on purpose, so that confession is always cheaper than being caught.

debates.bearing: The views are complementary. The fifth makes dishonesty costly, it recognises the loss the victim suffered, and the comparison with Exodus 22 shows God making it easier to confess than to keep hiding. Repentance for wrongs against others is more than a return to neutral; it is generous repair.

debates.question: Is the offering of Leviticus 5:1-13 a sin offering or a guilt offering?

views.label: A sin offering throughout
views.case: Verses 6, 7, 9, 11 and 12 all call it a sin offering, and verse 13 ties it to the grain offering rules. The word asham in verses 6 and 7 is best taken, as the BSB does in verse 7, as the penalty or reparation owed, 'as restitution for his sin,' not as the name of a separate sacrifice. The guilt offering proper begins at 5:14 with a ram and a fifth.

views.label: A transitional category
views.case: Others note that verse 6 does say 'his guilt offering' and that these cases share the language of guilt, 'he is guilty,' verses 2 to 5. They see 5:1-13 as a bridge where the two kinds of offering overlap, marking lapses that are both a defilement and a debt.

debates.bearing: The first view is the more natural reading of the rite, which follows the sin offering pattern. But the overlap of vocabulary is itself instructive: every sin both defiles and incurs a debt, and the two offerings are two angles on one problem.

debates.question: How can a handful of flour atone when Hebrews 9:22 says that 'without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness'?

views.label: An exception by mercy
views.case: Hebrews 9:22 itself says 'nearly everything' is purified with blood, allowing for exceptions. The flour offering is one, a concession for the destitute. God accepts less than the norm rather than let a person stay unforgiven.

views.label: Joined to the blood already on the altar
views.case: Others note that the memorial portion is burned 'atop the offerings made by fire to the LORD,' verse 12, on an altar already consecrated with blood. The poor man's flour is offered within the blood-based system, not outside it.

debates.bearing: Both views keep the principle intact. The flour did not create a bloodless way to God; it let the poorest Israelite share in the atonement the altar already provided. In the end, no Israelite offering removed sin by itself, Hebrews 10:4. Each one pointed to the blood of Christ.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb for 'acts unfaithfully,' ma'al, in 5:15 and 6:2, is the language of betrayal. It describes a wife who 'goes astray and is unfaithful' to her husband, Numbers 5:12, Achan taking what was devoted to God, Joshua 7:1, King Uzziah burning incense in the temple, 2 Chronicles 26:16-18, and the marriages Ezra confronted, Ezra 10:10. To misuse God's holy things or to cheat a neighbour under oath is not a technical slip. It is covenant disloyalty, the breach of a relationship.

The command 'he must confess,' 5:5, uses the reflexive stem of yadah, a verb whose causative stem means to give thanks or praise. The todah, the thanksgiving offering of Leviticus 7:12, comes from the same root. Confessing sin and praising God are related acts of acknowledgment: each says aloud what is true about God and about oneself. David joins them when he says, 'I will confess my transgressions to the LORD,' and then praises the God who 'forgave the guilt of my sin,' Psalm 32:5.

The phrase 'he shall bear the iniquity,' 5:1 and 5:17, joins the verb nasa, to lift or carry, with avon, iniquity. In the guilty person's case it means carrying the consequences of the sin. But Leviticus uses the same verb for the priests who eat the sin offering 'to take away the guilt of the congregation,' Leviticus 10:17, and for the goat that 'will carry on itself all their iniquities,' Leviticus 16:22. Isaiah uses it of the Servant who 'bore the sin of many,' Isaiah 53:12. Guilt must be carried by someone: either the sinner or a substitute.

The rash oath of 5:4, 'swears thoughtlessly,' uses bata, to speak rashly or blurt out. The same verb describes Moses at Meribah, who 'spoke rashly with his lips,' Psalm 106:33, and Proverbs warns that 'speaking rashly is like a piercing sword,' Proverbs 12:18. The law treats careless speech before God as a real offence.

The verb for 'make restitution' in 5:16 and 6:5 is shillem, the intensive stem of the root that also gives shalom. To repay is to make whole, to restore the peace a wrong has broken. 'In full,' 6:5, is literally 'by its head,' that is, the principal sum, to which the fifth is then added.

Finally, asham itself carries a range that the BSB reflects. It can mean the state of guilt, the compensation owed, or the ram offered. In 5:7 the BSB renders it 'restitution'; in 5:15 'guilt offering'; and the footnote at 5:19 gives 'he has paid full compensation' as an alternative to 'he was certainly guilty.' The one word links the guilt, the debt and the sacrifice that settles it.

typology.type: The sliding scale that reaches down to a day's flour, Leviticus 5:7-13
typology.fulfillment: God lowered the offering to what the poorest could bring, so poverty kept no one from forgiveness. The Gospels show Jesus' own family bringing the poor person's birds, Luke 2:24, so the Son of God entered the world among those this concession was written for. Paul draws the deeper line: 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. The escalation is that God does not merely lower the price; He pays it. The type falls short because the flour still had to be brought; in the gospel the gift is received with empty hands.

typology.type: The ram of the guilt offering, Leviticus 5:15 and 6:6
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 53:10 applies this very offering to the Servant: 'when His soul is made a guilt offering.' The ram repaid a debt to God's holiness; Christ's life does the same, not for one misused tithe but for the sin of many, Isaiah 53:12. Paul speaks of God 'having canceled the debt ascribed to us,' nailing it to the cross, Colossians 2:14. The type falls short in that the ram had to be valued in silver, and one ram answered one wrong. The Servant's worth is beyond valuation, and His offering answers every wrong.

typology.type: Restitution with a fifth added, Leviticus 5:16 and 6:5
typology.fulfillment: The wrongdoer had to restore more than he took. Psalm 69:4 gives the righteous sufferer's cry, 'Though I did not steal, I must repay,' in a psalm Jesus applies to Himself, John 15:25. Christ repays what He did not steal, and He repays with more than was lost. Paul's repeated 'how much more' in Romans 5:15-17 shows that the gift of grace outweighs the damage of Adam's trespass. The type falls short because the fifth was a set amount; in Christ the surplus of grace is beyond counting.

study.christ:
This passage leads to Christ first through Isaiah 53. The prophet did not choose a general word for sacrifice when he described the Servant's death; he chose the asham, 'when His soul is made a guilt offering,' Isaiah 53:10. That choice matters. The guilt offering is the sacrifice of reparation, for wrongs that cost God or a neighbour something real. By using it Isaiah says the cross does not only cleanse; it repays. What sin took from God's glory, Christ restores.

It leads to Christ through the problem of the unknown sin. Leviticus 5:17-19 covers the man who 'was unaware' but still 'guilty,' and requires a ram though he cannot even name what he did. The believer's position is the same. We do not know the full measure of our debts, but Christ's offering answers for them all. That is why the chapter's last word, forgiveness 'for anything he may have done to incur guilt,' 6:7, finds its fullness in Him.

It leads to Christ through poverty. The descent from lamb to birds to flour anticipates a Saviour born to parents who could only bring birds, Luke 2:24, and who 'became poor' so that the poor might be made rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9. In Leviticus the worshiper's poverty lowers the offering. In the gospel the Saviour's poverty lifts the worshiper.

It leads to Christ through restitution. Jesus insisted that worship waits on reconciliation, Matthew 5:23-24, repeating the order of 6:5-6. When Zacchaeus met Him, the tax collector's first response was to repay, Luke 19:8, and Jesus said, 'Today salvation has come to this house,' Luke 19:9. The grace of Christ does not cancel the duty to make things right; it creates the desire to do it.

It leads to Christ as the one who bears iniquity. Twice the passage says the guilty person 'shall bear the iniquity,' 5:1 and 5:17. Isaiah says of the Servant, 'He will bear their iniquities,' Isaiah 53:11. The burden that the law placed on the sinner, Christ lifts onto Himself.

The links must not be pressed too far. The two birds are not a hidden picture of the two natures of Christ, and the flour is not a code for His humanity. The connection rests on Isaiah's use of the asham, on the New Testament's teaching about restitution and poverty, and on the logic of guilt borne and debt repaid that the passage itself spells out.
study.god:
This passage shows God as the owner of all things. The 'holy things' of 5:15 belong to Him, and misusing them is a wrong against Him that needs compensation. But 6:2 goes further: cheating a neighbour is also 'unfaithfully against the LORD.' Every person's property sits under God's protection, and every oath invokes His name. There is no wrong so private that God is not a party to it.

It shows God as the one who remembers. Four times in 5:2-4 a person is unaware, and each time guilt remains until it is realised. God does not overlook what human memory loses. This is not pettiness. It is the faithfulness of a God whose justice does not decay with time, and who therefore also keeps His promises for ever.

It shows God as fair to the poor. He does not require of the destitute what He requires of the wealthy, and He does not give them a lesser forgiveness either. The lamb, the birds and the flour all end in 'he will be forgiven,' verses 10 and 13. The same God who elsewhere commands justice for the poor in the courts, Exodus 23:6, here makes sure they have equal access to the altar.

It shows God as a God of repair, not just pardon. He could have forgiven fraud without requiring anything of the offender, but that would have left the victim wronged. Instead He requires restitution, adds a fifth, and makes the victim whole before the ram is offered. The wronged neighbour matters to Him as much as the guilty worshiper does. And where no human heir remains, Numbers 5:8 says the payment goes to the LORD; no debt simply disappears.

It shows God as merciful to those who confess. The one who comes forward pays a fifth; the thief who is caught pays double, Exodus 22:4. God sets up His law so that honesty is rewarded and confession is always the better road.

For worship, the passage calls believers to a practical holiness: to keep their word, to speak up when truth is needed, to be careful with what belongs to God and others, and when they fail, to confess quickly and make it right generously, trusting a God who has already paid the greater debt in Christ.

crossReferences.note: The companion to Leviticus 6:1-7. It adds that the offender 'must confess the sin he has committed,' and that if the wronged person has no relative to receive the restitution, it goes to the LORD through the priest. The debt never simply lapses, and confession is an explicit part of repair.

Applies the rule of Leviticus 5:15-16 to a concrete case: anyone who eats a sacred offering in error must add a fifth to its value and give it to the priest. It shows what 'unfaithfully against the LORD's holy things' looked like in daily life, often a matter of carelessness rather than malice.

The civil penalties for theft: fourfold or fivefold for slaughtered livestock, double for stolen goods found or for a deposit dishonestly kept. Set beside Leviticus 6:5, where the man who confesses pays only the principal plus a fifth, it shows that the law made voluntary confession far less costly than being caught.

The Servant's soul is 'made a guilt offering,' and He 'will bear their iniquities' and 'bore the sin of many.' Isaiah takes the vocabulary of Leviticus 5, the asham and bearing iniquity, and applies it to one person whose death repays the debt of many and makes them righteous.

Jesus tells the worshiper who remembers a wronged brother to leave the gift at the altar, be reconciled, and then come back. It is the order of Leviticus 6:5-6, restitution to the neighbour first, then the offering, applied to the heart as well as the purse.

Zacchaeus promises to repay anyone he has cheated fourfold, well beyond the fifth of Leviticus 6:5 and matching the heavy penalty of Exodus 22:1. He sentences himself by the stricter law. Jesus answers, 'Today salvation has come to this house,' showing restitution as fruit of salvation, not its price.

Mary and Joseph offer 'a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons,' the offering of Leviticus 12:8 for those who cannot afford a lamb, the same concession found in Leviticus 5:7. Jesus is born into a household that lived at the level of this passage's mercy.

David describes the weight of unconfessed sin, then says, 'I will confess my transgressions to the LORD,' and 'You forgave the guilt of my sin.' It is the inner experience behind Leviticus 5:5, where the guilty person must confess before atonement is made.

'A partner to a thief hates his own soul; he receives the oath, but does not testify.' The proverb describes exactly the case of Leviticus 5:1: a person hears a public adjuration and keeps silent. Wisdom and law agree that silence can make one complicit.

Ezra charges the men who married foreign wives with being 'unfaithful,' the ma'al of Leviticus 5:15 and 6:2, and they present 'a ram from the flock as a guilt offering.' The returned exiles apply this passage to covenant disloyalty, pairing the offering with a costly change of life.

'Though I did not steal, I must repay.' The righteous sufferer is forced to make restitution for what he never took. Jesus applies this psalm to Himself, John 15:25, and the line captures the heart of the gospel's guilt offering: the innocent one repays the debt of the guilty.

'Though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor.' The descending scale of Leviticus 5:7-13 lowered the offering for the poor; Paul describes Christ lowering Himself so that the poor might be made rich, the ultimate answer to the worshiper who cannot afford a lamb.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning sin has been theft as well as rebellion. Adam and Eve took what was not given, Genesis 3:6, and every sin since has taken something from God's glory and often from a neighbour's good. The fall left a debt as well as a stain. This passage is where the law first names that debt and provides a way to repay it.

It answers the question raised by chapter 4. If sin pollutes God's dwelling, what about sin that also damages? Leviticus 5 and 6 reply that holiness requires both cleansing and repair. The ram atones, but the fifth restores. The neighbour is made whole, and so is the relationship with God.

It sets up what follows. Israel's prophets repeatedly charge the nation with ma'al, the unfaithfulness of this passage, and exile comes as the consequence of a debt too great to pay. Isaiah, looking beyond exile, sees a Servant whose soul is made a guilt offering, Isaiah 53:10, and who will justify many. The debt is to be paid, but not by Israel.

The story finds its answer at the cross. There Christ, who did not steal, repaid, Psalm 69:4. God canceled 'the debt ascribed to us,' Colossians 2:14. And the gift is greater than the loss, 'how much more,' Romans 5:15. Those who receive this grace become people who repay, like Zacchaeus, because they have been forgiven much.

The story ends in a new creation where nothing is owed and nothing is stolen. The 'holy things' will no longer be fenced off, for 'the throne of God and of the Lamb will be within the city, and His servants will worship Him,' Revelation 22:3. The restitution of all things will be complete, and every wrong ever done will have been either repaid in Christ or answered in judgment. What the fifth pointed to, a restoration greater than the loss, will be the shape of the whole renewed world.

quiz.q: What provision does God make for someone too poor to afford even two turtledoves or two young pigeons for the sin offering?

options.text: A tenth of an ephah of fine flour, with no oil or frankincense.
options.note: Verses 11 to 13 describe this final, most accessible level of provision.

options.text: He is exempt from bringing any offering.
options.note: The text scales the offering down rather than exempting anyone from bringing it.

options.text: He must wait until he can afford a lamb.
options.note: The provision allows immediate atonement at whatever level the person can afford, not a delay.

options.text: No further provision is made below the level of birds.
options.note: Verses 11 to 13 explicitly provide flour as a further accessible option.

quiz.q: What distinguishes the guilt offering, asham, from the ordinary sin offering in this passage?

options.text: It requires restitution, repaying the value plus a fifth, in addition to the sacrifice.
options.note: Verses 16 and 6:5 both specify this added restitution as unique to cases requiring the guilt offering.

options.text: It requires a more expensive animal in every case without exception.
options.note: While a ram is specified, the defining and unique feature is the restitution requirement, not merely the cost of the animal.

options.text: It can only be offered by priests.
options.note: The guilt offering is brought by the individual who sinned, not offered exclusively by priests.

options.text: There is no difference between the two offerings.
options.note: The restitution requirement clearly distinguishes the guilt offering from the sin offering.

quiz.q: What must someone do who has defrauded a neighbor through a false oath about lost property, according to Leviticus 6:1-7?

options.text: Return the property in full, add a fifth of its value, and bring a guilt offering to the priest.
options.note: Verses 4 to 6 describe exactly this combination of restitution and sacrifice.

options.text: Simply confess the sin with no further action required.
options.note: The passage requires both restitution and sacrifice, not confession alone.

options.text: Pay double the value of the property to the priest.
options.note: The text specifies a fifth added to the full value, paid to the wronged owner, not double payment to the priest.

options.text: No remedy is described for this situation.
options.note: Verses 1 to 7 give a detailed remedy for this exact situation.

quiz.q: What examples of guilt does Leviticus 5:1-4 list as requiring a sin offering?

options.text: Failing to testify as a witness, touching something unclean unknowingly, and swearing a rash oath.
options.note: Verses 1 to 4 list exactly these three categories of unintentional guilt.

options.text: Only deliberate murder and theft.
options.note: Those are serious deliberate sins addressed elsewhere; this passage concerns unintentional guilt.

options.text: Failing to pay the temple tax.
options.note: This is not among the cases listed in verses 1 to 4.

options.text: No specific examples are given.
options.note: Verses 1 to 4 give specific, concrete examples.

quiz.q: According to Isaiah 53:10, what does the prophet call the Suffering Servant's life given for sin?

options.text: A guilt offering, asham, the same term used throughout this Leviticus passage.
options.note: Isaiah 53:10 uses this specific sacrificial term to describe the Servant's atoning death.

options.text: A burnt offering only.
options.note: Isaiah's specific term is guilt offering, asham, not burnt offering, olah.

options.text: A peace offering.
options.note: Isaiah's term is specifically the guilt offering, not the peace offering.

options.text: No sacrificial term is used.
options.note: Isaiah 53:10 explicitly uses sacrificial language, asham, to describe the Servant's death.

questions: God scaled the offering down to whatever the poorest person could afford, even a handful of flour. Do you ever feel you cannot approach God because you have too little to offer Him?
Some guilt in this passage came from things done in complete unawareness, touching something unclean without realizing it. Where might you be guilty of something you have not yet even recognized?

The guilt offering required not just sacrifice but restitution, actually repairing the damage done. Is there a person you have wronged whom you need to actually repay or make right with, not just apologize to?
Restitution required paying back the full value plus a fifth, more than simply breaking even. Where might God be calling you to generosity in making amends, beyond the bare minimum?

Christ is called our guilt offering in Isaiah 53:10, His life given to settle our account with God completely. Do you live as though your account with God is truly settled, or do you still feel you owe Him something Christ has already paid?

translationNotes.note: Even if he is unaware of it shows that ceremonial and moral guilt in this system did not depend on conscious knowledge; unintentional contact still required atonement, underscoring the objective seriousness of sin and defilement.
The LORD's holy things likely refers to sacred offerings, tithes, or dedicated property; sinning against them, even unintentionally, required both restitution to the sanctuary and a guilt offering.

Add a fifth of the value reflects a consistent restitution formula appearing also in verse 16 and elsewhere in the law, compare Leviticus 27:13, establishing a standard penalty for wrongful use of another's property.
